name: Cluster API
lede: Clusters themselves as declarative, reconciled objects.
what: A SIG Cluster Lifecycle project with providers for AWS, vSphere, Nutanix and more, managing create, upgrade and delete of clusters through Kubernetes resources.
apart: One lifecycle model across on-prem and EKS, which is the answer to our hybrid shape. Versus eksctl and Terraform: reconciliation instead of a one-shot apply.
stand: The lifecycle half of fleet management, next to Auto Mode on EKS; automated fleet upgrades hang off it.
src: Cluster API maintainer track; Mirantis, Nutanix, Ericsson and Microsoft talks, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Delivery with ApplicationSets plus lifecycle with Cluster API is the whole answer to fleet toil.

name: Karmada
lede: A genuine multi-cluster scheduler, for workloads that must move.
what: A CNCF Incubating control plane that propagates workloads across clusters with placement policies, cluster affinities, failover with toleration windows, and replica division across survivors.
apart: It reschedules on cluster failure, which ApplicationSets can't. Bloomberg runs streaming on it for exactly that.
stand: Watch, until decision 2 says we have workloads that can't run active-active. If the list is empty, it stays here.
src: "Karmada Updates and Use Cases" (Bloomberg, Huawei), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Our notes had Karmada as a likely adopt. The live-live analysis is what moved it to watch.

name: Global Accelerator, Route 53, k8gb
lede: Three ways to move traffic off a dead region, and only one keeps DNS out of the RTO.
what: Global Accelerator: anycast IPs with failover at the AWS edge. Route 53: health-checked failover and latency records. k8gb: CNCF Incubating, Kubernetes-native global load balancing via CRDs.
apart: Global Accelerator doesn't change DNS, so client caching can't extend recovery, but it's AWS-only. Route 53 and k8gb are both DNS, so TTL is a floor. k8gb is the vendor-neutral one that also covers on-prem.
stand: Recommend Global Accelerator at the public edge with Route 53 behind it. ⚠️ Get the real failover time and the cost from AWS first.
src: "k8gb Is Growing Up"; "Building Resilient DNS Infrastructure at Scale", KubeCon NA 2026
note: Decision 2a. What settles it is whether on-prem needs the same mechanism.

name: Velero
lede: Backup and restore for cluster resources and volumes.
what: A CNCF tool that backs up Kubernetes resources and persistent volumes to object storage, with scheduled backups, CSI snapshots, and restore into the same or a different cluster.
apart: The project update headline: faster backups, consistent snapshots, incremental everything. Versus Kasten: open source, but less app-aware. A Data Protection WG is standardising what's underneath.
stand: Adopt, and put restore drills on the calendar: a backup nobody has restored is a hope.
src: Velero project update (Red Hat); Kubernetes Data Protection WG, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Pair with reclaimPolicy Retain on stateful storage classes: the storage layer is the first line, backups the second.

name: External Secrets, Infisical, Vault, OpenBao
lede: A sync layer first, so the secret store becomes a reversible choice.
what: External Secrets Operator syncs secrets from any backend into Kubernetes Secrets. Infisical is an open-core secrets platform with agent-aware features. OpenBao is the Linux Foundation fork of Vault.
apart: ESO decouples workloads from the store, so changing stores is a config change. Infisical has the friendliest UX; OpenBao is the drop-in path from Vault with an open licence.
stand: Adopt ESO now; decide the store after inventorying long-lived secrets. The direction is fewer long-lived secrets at all. On no path, but on a clock.
src: "Kubernetes Secrets Were a Bad Idea. Now What?" (RBC); Infisical demo, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Sequencing turns a strategic decision into a preference.

name: OpenTelemetry and Jaeger
lede: The default telemetry pipeline, and where cardinality cost is won or lost.
what: OpenTelemetry: vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs and the Collector for traces, metrics and logs. Jaeger: the CNCF tracing backend, now built on the OTel Collector.
apart: 38 sessions mentioned OTel versus 17 for Prometheus directly. The scale lesson every time: two-stage aggregation and OTTL in the Collector cut series counts before they cost money.
stand: Adopt the OTel conventions as they are. Watch the trap: switching to delta temporality breaks every rate() query.
note: Yahoo: 86% fewer series and roughly 140 thousand dollars a year saved on one cluster.

name: OpenCost
lede: Cost allocation per namespace, label and team, CNCF-native.
what: A CNCF project that allocates cluster spend (compute, storage, network) to Kubernetes objects using cloud billing and on-prem rate cards.
apart: An open specification, vendor-neutral, works on-prem. ArgoCon showed it inside the Argo CD UI, so cost shows up at deploy time rather than in a monthly report.
stand: Trial after tag and label discipline; without labels every cost tool draws the same unattributable chart.
src: ArgoCon cost intelligence; "From Packets to Paychecks" (Adobe), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Cost at the point of deploy changes behaviour; a monthly FinOps deck doesn't.

name: Network Flow Monitor vs eBPF
lede: Two ways to attribute network traffic and cost: run one, not both.
what: NFM is the EKS Container Network Observability add-on: a node agent reporting top flows plus ENA allowance counters. eBPF tools, like Cilium's Hubble or Adobe's pipeline, read flows in-kernel.
apart: NFM is lowest effort on EKS and exposes allowance-exceeded counters nothing else reports, but it's AWS-only, capped near 5,000 nodes, and blind to host-network pods. eBPF covers on-prem too.
stand: Decision 8. ⚠️ Confirm the add-on name and pricing before enabling it fleet-wide.
src: EKS network observability docs; "From Packets to Paychecks" (Adobe), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Per-namespace egress and retransmits also make a cheap, app-agnostic canary signal. That's our idea, to test.

name: Crossplane
lede: Cloud resources and app infrastructure as Kubernetes APIs we define.
what: A CNCF Graduated control plane: providers manage cloud resources; compositions and functions turn them into our own typed APIs. v2 lets compositions include plain Kubernetes resources.
apart: Multi-cloud managed resources plus a function pipeline for platform logic. Versus Terraform: continuous reconciliation. Versus kro: kro composes but doesn't manage cloud resources, and now runs inside Crossplane.
stand: Trial, starting with S3, aiming at the app layer. We already contribute to function-lifecycle.
src: Crossplane Contribfest (Upbound); "What Changes When Crossplane Adoption Gets Real" (American Family), KubeCon NA 2026
note: The real decision is the CDK-to-Crossplane seam: decision 3.

name: kro
lede: Lightweight resource-graph composition with YAML and CEL.
what: Kube Resource Orchestrator: ResourceGraphDefinitions turn a group of Kubernetes resources into one custom API, wired together with CEL.
apart: Composition without the weight of a full Crossplane install; backed by AWS, Google and Microsoft, and pairs with ACK on EKS. Through function-kro it also runs inside Crossplane.
stand: Watch. Relevant if Crossplane's weight becomes the objection, and less either-or than it looked last year. ⚠️ Check its release and stability first.
src: "Achieving Cross-Cloud Portability with kro"; Crossplane function-kro, KubeCon NA 2026
note: EKS Capabilities ships a managed kro, which is worth trying alongside the Auto Mode work.

name: Karpenter, KEDA and VPA
lede: Nodes, signals and pod size: three layers, three tools.
what: Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes fast. KEDA scales workloads on external signals like Kafka lag or Prometheus queries. VPA, now with in-place pod resize, adjusts requests without restarts.
apart: KEDA reacts to the signal we actually care about, not CPU. In-place resize changes the HPA and VPA calculus. Letting all three act on one workload is how autoscalers fight.
stand: Trial KEDA on one Kafka consumer: KEDA for the signal, VPA for the size, Karpenter (or Auto Mode) for nodes.
src: "Autoscaling at Scale with KEDA" (Stripe); "In-Place Pod Resizing Like I'm 5" (AWS), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Our brainstorm idea, Prometheus and Kafka lag into scaling, is exactly KEDA's job, not a custom controller.

name: Backstage
lede: The open-source developer portal most of the industry starts from.
what: A CNCF Incubating framework from Spotify: software catalog, scaffolder templates, TechDocs and a large plugin ecosystem, assembled into an internal portal.
apart: The most flexible, with the largest community; BackstageCon was a full day. But it's a TypeScript application we'd build, upgrade and staff, not an install.
stand: Decide after the paved road works. The catalog and the placement vocabulary carry the value, and can exist before any portal.
src: BackstageCon; "Backstage's Role in AI-Assisted Development" (DoorDash, Spotify), KubeCon NA 2026
note: The question to ask of any portal: who maintains the plugins, and does it actually deploy anything?
